fetched_contents.text: The action of fillers in the enhancement of the tribological performance of epoxy composite coatings 1. Introduction Polymers are increasingly being used as alternatives to metals in industrial applications due to better corrosion resistance and excellent strength to weight ratio. Despite light weight and good machinability, their use is restricted in applications involving wear. To overcome this limitation, polymers can be reinforced with fillers to increase the wear resistance of the composites depending on: particle type [1]; particle size and size distribution [2]; interfacial actions between filler and matrix resin [3]; particle content and particles dispersion level in the composite [4]; and wear test conditions such as: the wear mode (pin-on-disc, Taber Abraser, etc.) [5], counter-body [6], sliding velocity and sliding distance [7,8], applied load and test temperature [9,10]. The tribology of polymers does not follow the laws of friction as known for metals, and the coefficient of friction μ depends on various factors [2,11], such as normal load, sliding speed, temperature (polymers have much lower melting points), and glass transition temperature, Tg. For example, the semi-crystalline to amorphous phase transition of the polymers is often not considered, particularly for surface layers. Epoxy (EP) presents several advantages among polymers including superior temperature stability, high adhesive ability, and considerable solvent resistance. All these properties make it a suitable candidate as matrix for polymer coatings. However, the practical use of epoxy coatings in industry is limited by its poor tribological properties of epoxy (low wear and impact resistance), due to its three-dimensional network structure when compared to thermoplastics [12,13]. To meet the tribological demands of various working conditions, fillers must be incorporated to formulate wear resistant composite materials. Filled epoxy composites offer advantages such as high corrosion resistance, when compared to metals. Combining the advantages of the individual constituents (the good specific strength and thermal properties of the neat epoxy and the superior wear resistance of the fillers), the filled epoxy composites form an attractive class of materials [1]. Conventional inorganic fillers, such as SiO2 or SiC, have been proven to effectively improve the wear resistance and mechanical strength of neat epoxy resin. Ceramics have good thermal and wear resistance and even small amounts and small particle sizes of such reinforcements can improve strength and fracture toughness [14]. Kang et al. [15] showed that nano-SiO2 fillers (average diameter 20–30 nm) lowered the friction coefficient and decreased the wear rate of unfilled epoxy resin. Other researchers proved that the silica filler with smaller particle size was effective in improving the wear resistance of the silica/epoxy composites [16]. The high specific strength and specific modulus of SiC fillers has been recognized by many and used in various studies for improving the tribological properties of EP [[17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22]]. Suresha et al. [23] fabricated EP-SiC-GF composites with greatly improved mechanical strength and wear resistance in dry sliding conditions, while other researchers proved that by reinforcing glass-epoxy composites with SiC fillers, the three-body abrasive wear was significantly reduced [24]. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a commercially used filler, is known to reduce the adhesion and the friction coefficient [27]. Addition of PTFE as a solid lubricant, as well as nano-CuO fillers, to an epoxy resin helped in stabilizing the transfer film created by the incorporated PTFE, thereby decreasing friction and wear of the investigated epoxy [28]. Polyethylene (PE) is usually being used as a thermoplastic filler to improve the fracture properties of thermoset resins, which are extremely vulnerable to impact-induced damage because of their highly cross-linked structure [29]. Wollastonite has been shown to improve the mechanical properties of epoxy resin such as impact, tensile and flexural strength [30]. In a study by Xian et al. wollastonite fillers enhanced the wear resistance and reduced the sliding coefficient of friction of an epoxy resin, proving that wollastonite with fine particle sizes (2–8 μm) contributed to the formation of an effective transfer film responsible for the improved tribological properties [31]. In the present work, the focus was set on developing epoxy formulations with the specific use as coatings for roll covers in the paper machine industry [32]. In a paper machine, rolls are subject to high mechanical, thermal and chemical stresses, whereby the uniform surface condition and cleanliness are essential for the production process, as explained in detail in a previous work [33]. The fibrous raw materials, fillers, chemical additives and possibly recycled paper used in the paper pose a high risk of adhering on the roll surfaces. As a result, faults in the process are encountered, and the roll surface must be cleaned continuously [34]. A concept for a roll coating with sufficiently good non-stick properties, combined with good mechanical resistance gives clear advantages in the application of such coatings. The main goal of the present work was to evaluate the influence of fillers and additives on the wear resistance and anti-stick properties of epoxy resins. As a result, prototype rolls with different requirements were produced and used in cooperation with machine manufacturers under operating conditions. fetched_contents.text: A review on tribology of polymer composite coatings Outline Show full outline Hide outline Show {{imgMenuList.length - 9}} more figures Hide {{imgMenuList.length - 9}} figures Show {{tableMenuList.length - 5}} more tables Hide {{tableMenuList.length - 5}} tables Outline Show full outline Hide outline Show {{imgMenuList.length - 9}} more figures Hide {{imgMenuList.length - 9}} figures Show {{tableMenuList.length - 5}} more tables Hide {{tableMenuList.length - 5}} tables Review Article | Open Access Lin ZHANG1, Guoxin XIE1( ), Zhanbo LI1, Hao CHEN1, Hanjun GONG1, Wenhu XU2, Dan GUO1, Jianbin LUO1( ) 1 State Key Laboratory of Tribology, Department of Mechanical Engineering , Tsinghua University , Beijing 100084 , China 2 School of Mechatronics Engineering, Key Laboratory of Tribology, Nanchang University, Nanchang , Jiangxi 33003 , China Show Author Information Abstract Self-lubricating polymer composite coatings, with tailorable tribological and mechanical properties, have been widely employed on mechanical parts to reduce friction and wear, which saves energy and improves the overall performance for applications such as aerospace satellite parts, shafts, gears, and bushings. The addition of functional fillers can overcome the limitations of single-polymer coatings and extend the service life of the coatings by providing a combination of low friction, high wear resistance, high load bearing, high temperature resistance, and high adhesion. This paper compares the heat resistance, and the tribological and mechanical properties of common polymer matrices, as well as the categories of functional fillers that improve the coating performance. Applicable scopes, process parameters, advantages, and limitations of the preparation methods of polymer coatings are discussed in detail. The tribological properties of the composite coatings with different matrices and fillers are compared, and the lubrication mechanisms are analyzed. Fillers reduce friction by promoting the formation of transfer films or liquid shear films. Improvement of the mechanical properties of the composite coatings with fillers of different morphologies is described in terms of strengthening and toughening mechanisms, including a stress transfer mechanism, shear yielding, crack bridging, and interfacial debonding. The test and enhancement methods for the adhesion properties between the coating and substrate are discussed. The coating adhesion can be enhanced through mechanical treatment, chemical treatment, and energy treatment of the substrate. Finally, we propose the design strategies for high-performance polymer composite coating systems adapted to specific operating conditions, and the limitations of current polymer composite coating research are identified. fetched_contents.text: Influence of the Filler Particles’ Surface Morphology on the Polyurethane Matrix’s Structure Formation in the Composite Abstract This article presents the surface morphology effect of silicon carbide (SiC) particles on the polyurethane binder’s structure formation in a dispersed-filled composite. Fillers improve the tribological performance of polymer composite coatings by reducing friction and wear resistance, with the exact effects depending on filler type, load, and dispersion quality. The direct evidence shows that polymer fillers can form a tribofilm under dry sliding, which improves wear behavior, and that wear degree is inversely proportional to particle size in some cases [N1-F1]. A review of polymer composite coatings likewise notes that functional fillers can reduce friction by promoting transfer films or liquid shear films, and that composites can provide a combination of low friction, high wear resistance, high load bearing, and other desirable properties [N3-F2]. The same review also emphasizes that tribological properties are strongly influenced by the type, size, and dispersion of fillers, as well as test conditions such as sliding velocity, applied load, and temperature [N3-F2].

Filler type is a key determinant of tribological behavior. In the epoxy-coating evidence, conventional inorganic fillers such as SiO₂ or SiC improve wear resistance and mechanical strength, while PTFE, nano-SiO₂, and nano-CuO can lower friction coefficient and decrease wear rate [N1-F1]. The graphene-enhanced coating study likewise shows that adding 4.0 wt% graphene can reduce the friction coefficient and wear rate by 80% and 76% respectively, and that graphene can form a self-lubricating transfer film during friction [N5-F4]. These examples support the idea that specific filler chemistry and structure can directly alter tribological response, often by changing the contact interface behavior.

Load and dispersion are equally important. The epoxy-coating review notes that tribology of polymers depends on normal load, sliding speed, temperature, and glass transition temperature, and that filler incorporation must consider particle size, size distribution, interfacial actions, particle content, and dispersion level [N1-F1]. The same source also states that wear degree is inversely proportional to particle size, indicating that smaller fillers can be more effective in some contexts [N1-F1]. A related point is that poor dispersion can be detrimental: the review of polymer composite coatings explicitly states that fillers usually aggregate with a relatively large size and are poorly dispersed in the polymer matrix, which is unfavorable for enhancing mechanical properties [N5-F4]. This suggests that dispersion quality strongly affects whether tribological improvements are realized.

The mechanisms by which fillers improve tribology include lubrication, load transfer, and wear debris formation. The review explicitly identifies transfer films and liquid shear films as lubrication mechanisms [N3-F2]. The epoxy-coating evidence also describes that fillers can form a tribofilm under dry sliding, which improves wear behavior [N1-F1]. Load transfer is implied by the discussion of interfacial actions and the role of fillers in strengthening and toughening mechanisms [N3-F2]. Wear debris formation is indirectly supported by the observation that filler migration and peeling can occur at the friction surface, leading to microstresses and polymer deformation [N1-F1]. This indicates that tribological improvements are not just surface-level; they involve interactions between the filler, matrix, and sliding interface, with debris formation sometimes acting as both a degradation pathway and a mechanism for local load redistribution.

Overall, fillers improve tribological performance by forming protective tribofilms, reducing direct sliding resistance, and altering the frictional contact state through chemistry, size, dispersion, and load conditions [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4].

Polymer composites generally outperform single polymer coatings under tribological conditions, especially when wear resistance and friction reduction are the goals. The review of polymer composite coatings states that self-lubricating composites can show low COF and low wear, while single-polymer coatings often lack these properties [N3-F2]. It also notes that composites can provide high load-bearing, high temperature resistance, and high adhesion, which are important in tribological applications [N3-F2]. The graphene-enhanced coating study similarly compares filled polymer coatings to neat epoxy and shows that adding 4.0 wt% graphene substantially lowers friction and wear, demonstrating a clear tribological advantage of composites [N5-F4]. The epoxy-coating review further states that fillers can improve wear resistance and mechanical strength, and that filled epoxy composites combine the advantages of neat epoxy with the superior wear resistance of fillers [N1-F1].

Composites outperform single polymers most clearly where tribological durability and multifunctionality matter. The review highlights that polymer composites are replacing metallic components in bearings, housings, and flexures because of lower weight and better frictional properties [N1-R2]. It also states that composites can extend service life by providing low friction, high wear resistance, high load bearing, high temperature resistance, and high adhesion [N3-F2]. These advantages are especially relevant in coatings, where the surface must withstand repeated sliding, heat, and chemical exposure [N3-F2]. The graphene study reinforces this by showing that composites can maintain low friction and wear even under elevated temperatures, where neat polymer coatings might degrade [N5-F4].

Single polymers, however, can still retain advantages such as flexibility, processing ease, and some inherent chemical stability. The epoxy-coating review notes that epoxy has superior temperature stability, high adhesive ability, and considerable solvent resistance, making it a suitable matrix for coatings [N1-F1]. The same source also says that the practical use of epoxy coatings is limited by poor tribological properties, not by its chemical advantages [N1-F1]. This implies that single polymers may be preferable when tribological demands are low or when other properties such as adhesion, flexibility, or chemical resistance are more important than wear resistance. The review of polymer composite coatings likewise notes that polymer coatings can have weak wear resistance, more wear debris, and a more fragile surface layer compared to harder coatings such as ceramics or carbon-based coatings [N3-F2]. So, single polymers may remain useful when the application does not require extreme tribological performance.

The practical implications for coating design and application are that composites are better suited to harsh, wear-intensive environments, while single polymers may be more attractive where processing simplicity, flexibility, or chemical compatibility are priorities [N3-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence suggests a trade-off: composites can improve tribological performance but may require careful filler selection, dispersion control, and process optimization to avoid drawbacks such as brittleness or delamination [N3-F2][N5-F4]. This means that the choice between composite and single-polymer coatings depends on the specific operating conditions and performance requirements of the application.

Fillers improve the mechanical properties of polymer composite coatings by increasing hardness, stiffness, modulus, and toughness, but the extent of improvement depends on filler loading and matrix-filler compatibility. The direct evidence states that the mechanical characteristics of polymer composite materials are strongly dependent on the mechanical strength, hardness, and stiffness of the fillers [N2-R3]. It also notes that the incorporation of wood apple shell particles increases tensile strength, flexural strength, erosive wear resistance, and viscoelastic stiffness [N2-R4]. Another source says that modulus is one of the basic properties of composites and that the goal of using particulate fillers is often to increase it [N2-R5]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that fillers can meaningfully enhance mechanical rigidity and strength.

Filler loading affects mechanical response in a non-linear way. The review of polymer composite coatings states that the addition of functional fillers can improve mechanical properties, and that the tribological and mechanical properties of common polymer matrices are compared in the paper [N3-F2]. The epoxy-coating evidence similarly notes that fillers must be incorporated to formulate wear-resistant composite materials, with the advantages of the individual constituents depending on particle type, size, size distribution, interfacial actions, particle content, and dispersion level [N1-F1]. The graphene-enhanced coating study shows that 4.0 wt% graphene significantly improves micro-hardness and thermo-gravimetric properties, and that increasing filler loading can reduce friction and wear [N5-F4]. These examples indicate that higher loading can improve mechanical properties, but the optimal level depends on the matrix and filler combination.

Matrix-filler compatibility is a critical factor. The epoxy-coating review emphasizes that tribology depends on interfacial actions between filler and matrix resin [N1-F1]. A separate review on polymer/filler composites states that the performance of polymer composites depends not only on the intrinsic properties of fillers and matrix but also on interfacial bonding [N4-R2]. The polyurethane surface-morphology study further explains that the polymer matrix should be considered as the sum of three constituent elements, including the boundary layer, transition layer, and bulk matrix, and that the structure and properties of these layers differ from the polymer in volume [N4-F3]. This means that good compatibility can improve load transfer, reduce voids, and strengthen the overall composite response. The surface-functionalization evidence also notes that covalent or non-covalent bonds can improve physical and mechanical properties by limiting polymer chain mobility and increasing glass transition temperature [N4-F3].

However, there are trade-offs such as brittleness or delamination under stress. The review of polymer composite coatings states that polymer composites can have weak wear resistance, more wear debris, and a more fragile surface layer compared to harder coatings [N3-F2]. The graphene study also notes that some polymer coatings have disadvantages such as low hardness and high temperature creep, and that thermostability and tribological properties can deteriorate in extreme environments [N5-F4]. The filler-matrix compatibility evidence further implies that poor dispersion can be unfavorable for mechanical properties [N5-F4]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that fillers can strengthen coatings, but only if they are well dispersed, compatibly bonded, and loaded at an optimal level; otherwise, brittleness, delamination, or reduced toughness may appear.

Filler selection, dispersion, and processing together shape coating performance by influencing filler morphology, particle size, surface chemistry, and interfacial bonding. The evidence shows that the performance of polymer composites depends on filler morphology, surface chemistry, and interfacial compatibility with the polymer matrix [N4-R4]. The polyurethane surface-morphology study explicitly states that the filler particles’ surface morphology affects the polyurethane matrix’s structure formation, and that surface relief has a strong effect on molecular mobility and boundary-layer behavior [N4-F3]. It also notes that the morphology of the filler particles’ surface does not affect the dependence of boundary-layer thickness on filler volume fraction, but that increased surface development reduces boundary-layer thickness [N4-F3]. This means that particle shape and surface detail can alter how the matrix behaves near the filler interface.

Particle size is another key factor. The epoxy-coating evidence states that wear degree is inversely proportional to particle size, implying that smaller particles can improve tribological performance [N1-F1]. The same source also emphasizes that particle size and size distribution are important variables in tribology [N1-F1]. The review of polymer composite coatings similarly notes that the type and size of fillers strongly influence tribological performance [N5-F4]. Taken together, these sources support the conclusion that particle size affects both tribological response and mechanical behavior, with smaller particles often being more effective in some applications.

Surface chemistry is important because it governs filler-matrix interactions. The filler-matrix compatibility evidence states that the performance of polymer composites depends on interfacial bonding [N4-R2]. The surface-functionalization study explains that covalent or non-covalent functionalization can improve interfacial interactions and that such treatments can increase glass transition temperature and improve physical and mechanical properties [N4-F3]. The review on polymer/filler composites also states that the performance is governed by particle morphology, surface chemistry, and interfacial compatibility [N4-R4]. This means that chemical modifications can improve adhesion and transfer load more effectively than geometry alone.

Processing conditions strongly affect filler dispersion and interfacial bonding. The filler-matrix compatibility evidence notes that the filler surface requires careful evaluation using suitable analysis methods to ensure effective interaction [N4-F3]. The nanoparticle-dispersion evidence says that the quality of nanoparticle dispersion can modify matrix morphology differently and ultimately alter deformation behavior [N6-R1]. The elastomer nanocomposites evidence adds that the main effect of rigid particles in a soft polymeric medium is an increase in composite stiffness [N6-R2]. The filler-dispersed effect evidence similarly states that deformation before failure is reduced in filled composites, implying that processing can change how the material deforms under stress [N6-R4]. These sources collectively show that processing conditions determine how well fillers are dispersed and how strongly they bond with the matrix.

Good dispersion and compatibility improve both tribology and mechanics. The review of polymer composite coatings states that transfer films or liquid shear films are formed when fillers are well incorporated, which reduces friction [N3-F2]. It also states that fillers can improve mechanical properties and that the tribological and mechanical properties of common polymer matrices are compared in the paper [N3-F2]. The epoxy-coating evidence explicitly links particle type, size, size distribution, interfacial actions, particle content, and dispersion level to tribological behavior [N1-F1]. The graphene study shows that 4.0 wt% graphene improves micro-hardness and thermo-gravimetric properties, reinforcing the idea that good dispersion and compatibility are necessary for mechanical and tribological gains [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a unified conclusion: better filler selection, better dispersion, and better processing lead to stronger, more durable coatings with improved tribology and mechanics [N4-R4][N6-R2][N6-R1][N3-F2][N1-F1].

## Integrated explanation of how fillers improve tribological and mechanical properties of polymer composite coatings compared to single polymer materials

Fillers improve polymer composite coatings by strengthening the material and making it more durable under friction and wear, while also often improving hardness, stiffness, and toughness. At the same time, the choice of filler, its dispersion quality, and the way the coating is made all shape whether the improvements are realized. Compared to single polymer materials, composites are especially attractive when tribological durability is needed, but single polymers may still be preferred when flexibility, chemical compatibility, or processing simplicity matter [N3-F2][N1-F1][N5-F4].

### 1) Tribological improvements from fillers

Fillers improve tribological performance mainly by reducing friction and wear resistance. The evidence shows that polymer fillers can form a tribofilm under dry sliding, which improves wear behavior [N1-F1]. A review of polymer composite coatings likewise states that functional fillers can reduce friction by promoting transfer films or liquid shear films, and that composites can provide a combination of low friction, high wear resistance, high load-bearing, and other desirable properties [N3-F2]. The same review also emphasizes that tribological properties depend strongly on filler type, size, and dispersion, as well as test conditions such as sliding velocity, applied load, and temperature [N3-F2].

The exact tribological effects depend on filler type. In the epoxy-coating evidence, conventional inorganic fillers such as SiO₂ or SiC improve wear resistance and mechanical strength, while PTFE, nano-SiO₂, and nano-CuO can lower the friction coefficient and decrease wear rate [N1-F1]. The graphene-enhanced coating study likewise shows that adding 4.0 wt% graphene can reduce the friction coefficient and wear rate by 80% and 76% respectively, and that graphene can form a self-lubricating transfer film during friction [N5-F4]. These examples show that the chemical identity and structure of the filler matter deeply to tribological response.

Load and dispersion quality are also central. The epoxy-coating review notes that tribology depends on normal load, sliding speed, temperature, and glass transition temperature, and that filler incorporation must consider particle size, size distribution, interfacial actions, particle content, and dispersion level [N1-F1]. The same source also states that wear degree is inversely proportional to particle size, indicating that smaller particles can be more effective in some contexts [N1-F1]. The graphene study adds that poor dispersion can be unfavorable for mechanical properties, reinforcing the idea that dispersion quality strongly determines whether tribological improvements are realized [N5-F4].

The mechanisms by which fillers improve tribology include lubrication, load transfer, and wear debris formation. Transfer films and liquid shear films are explicit lubrication mechanisms [N3-F2]. The epoxy-coating evidence also describes that fillers can form a tribofilm under dry sliding, which improves wear behavior [N1-F1]. Load transfer is implied by the discussion of interfacial actions and strengthening/toughening mechanisms [N3-F2]. Wear debris formation is indirectly supported by the observation that filler migration and peeling can occur at the friction surface, leading to microstresses and polymer deformation [N1-F1]. ### 2) Mechanical improvements from fillers

## Integrated explanation of how fillers improve tribological and mechanical properties of polymer composite coatings compared to single polymer materials

Fillers improve polymer composite coatings by strengthening the material and making it more durable under friction and wear, while also often improving hardness, stiffness, and toughness.
